label: Start
description: The entry point of a workflow. Every flow requires exactly one. Compiles to a Void start marker in Inflowenger.

label: Wait for All
description: A synchronisation barrier — the flow equivalent of JavaScript `Promise.all` or WaitGroup in Golang .When a node fans out to several outbound branches, the Inflowenger runtime launches them all in parallel and they run simultaneously. Most of the time each branch simply flows on with the context it already has. But when a later step must not start until every one of those parallel branches has finished, place a `Wait for All` in front of it: it holds until all inbound branches complete, merges each of their results into the shared context, and only then continues with the fully-updated context. Compiles to a Void node whose `depend` is the set of all inbound nodes.

label: Continue After
description: Park the flow and resume it at a scheduled time. Compiles to an Extrinsic against `svc.continue.at`, which records the captured outbound nodes and re-launches them at the given time. The delay/at inputs resolve to a single unix time (absolute at compile time, or `now + delay` at run time).

label: Goto
description: Transfer control to a node in another (or the same) workflow, like a subroutine jump. Compiles to a GoTo.
notes: A Goto is a subroutine call: control jumps to the target node in the target flow, and when that flow reaches the Goto's end node it continues to whatever follows the Goto. Each Goto runs its own private copy of the flow it calls, so several branches may enter one Goto, two Gotos may call the same flow and even share an end node, and the called flow's own wiring is left untouched for anything else that uses it.

Two things to keep in mind: the target flow is loaded once per Goto node, so it costs a copy of that flow (do not reach for a Goto to save re-drawing one or two nodes), and nesting is bounded — a Goto that jumps back into a flow already being called re-enters the same copy rather than nesting deeper, which is what makes a loop through a Goto terminate.

label: LLM
description: Call a language model. Its required global config comes from a settings profile (the inflowv1 plugin settings); `body` holds the prompt template. Each bound function becomes an output port the model can route through. Compiles to a Plugin node.
notes: Init messages: use the shorthand `"system": "…"` and `"prompt": "…"` on `data` instead of writing body.messages by hand.

Each bound function is `{ "name": "snake_case_tool_name", "title": "Label", "description": "when the model should call this", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { … }, "required": [] } }`.
`name` is both the tool name and the route tag, `description` is what the model chooses on (always write one), `parameters` is the JSON Schema of the call arguments (flat properties only).

`body.clear_history` (default false): OFF the node RESUMES its conversation across runs — the init messages seed it once and later runs add no new user turn. Set it TRUE for any node inside a LOOP, or the `prompt` template is never re-evaluated after the first pass: the model answers from stale history, the conversation grows every run, and the loop cannot change its own outcome. The conversation lives on the node's scope, so it also outlives the process.

label: Rule
description: Evaluate a rule (JavaScript or OPA/Rego) over the scoped context and route through matching handlers. The scoped slice arrives as `input`; in JavaScript the LAST EXPRESSION is the decision (not a `return`), in Rego it is the variable named by the result variable. Compiles to a Contract; each handler is an output port for a routed branch.

dataFields.logic_rule:
let scopedData = input // the slice selected by `scope`

// Return the NAME of the handler to fire, as a string — decide on every path.
let decision = scopedData.ok ? 'approved' : 'rejected'

decision // last expression — this is the routed decision

notes: Handlers are `{ "id": "h1", "name": "approved", "title": "Approved" }`; each is a routed branch.
`name` is the branch's route tag — the decision has to fire it and the edge leaving that port carries it — while `title` only labels the port on the canvas.
`logic_rule` is JS (`lang: "js"`) whose last expression is the decision, or Rego (`lang: "opa"`) where `opa_result` names the variable holding it.

The decision MUST be one string equal to a handler `name` (or an array of handler names to fire several ports at once). Anything else — an unknown string, `''`, `null`, `undefined`, an object such as `{ pass: true }` — fires no handler, which prunes every outgoing edge and ends that branch silently: no error, no log line.

Make the decision exhaustive over the handlers: `let decision = ok ? 'approved' : 'rejected'`, never `let decision; if (ok) { decision = 'approved' }` — the else path returns `undefined` and is a dead port that looks fine on the canvas.

label: MCP
description: Connect to an MCP server as a client. In "Tool only" mode it calls a single tool; in "With LLM" mode it drives a model (provider config from a settings profile) that binds and calls the loaded tools internally — tool routing never surfaces as workflow edges. Connection params (URL, transport, auth) are set on the node. Compiles to a Plugin node.
notes: An MCP node runs in one of two modes; set `mcpMode` and keep `request` in step:

- `mcpMode: "tool"` (`request: "call_tool"`) — tool-only, an integration: it calls ONE named tool on the server and returns its result, no model involved. Set `tool` to the tool name once its tools are loaded from the server in the app; `arguments` are shaped by that tool's input schema. Use this when the step is a single deterministic call.

- `mcpMode: "llm"` (`request: "run"`) — driven by a model: it binds ALL of the server's tools and lets the model call them itself over a conversation. Seed it with the `system` / `prompt` shorthand (same as an LLM node); the provider/model come from a settings profile. Tool calls stay inside the node — they never surface as workflow edges — so this node has a single output. Use this when a task needs a model to decide which of the server's tools to call.

`functions` is the tools the model MAY call — a whitelist, not a catalogue. EMPTY binds every tool the server advertises; a non-empty list binds only those names and the node REFUSES any other call at run time. Restrict it when the task is read-only and the server also offers write or shell tools. The live input schemas are re-fetched from the server each run, so only the names matter here.

`body.clear_history` (default false): OFF the node RESUMES its conversation across runs. Set it TRUE for any node inside a LOOP, or the `prompt` template is never re-evaluated after the first pass — the model answers from stale history and the loop cannot change its own outcome. The conversation lives on the node's scope, so it also outlives the process.

`body.max_tool_turns` (default 8): the cap on agentic turns, one turn being one model call plus the tools it asked for. The backend floors it at the default, so a value at or below 8 is the same as leaving it out — only a HIGHER value takes effect. Raise it for multi-step work.
In BOTH modes the node has ONE untagged output: it derives no ports, so tool calls never become edges and there is nothing to tag. Do not put a `port` on the edge leaving it.

Unlike an `llm` or `ai-decision` node it has NO `_exception` port, and its single edge fires whether the call succeeded or failed. A failed node commits `{ "error": "…" }` to its `key`, so the NEXT node must test that error itself — there is no error branch to catch it.

label: JS
description: Run a JavaScript step against the scoped context and write the result back to `key`. The scoped slice arrives as `input`, and the value of the LAST EXPRESSION in the code is the node output — not a `return` statement. Compiles to a Code node (variant `js`) in the Inflowenger ecosystem.

label: OPA
description: Evaluate an OPA/Rego policy against the scoped context and write the selected result back to `key`. Inside the policy the given scope is accessible through the `input` key (e.g. `input.<field in scope>`), and the key/value pairs defined in Conditions are accessible through the `data` key (e.g. `data.<condition key>`). Try your policy in the playground: https://play.openpolicyagent.org. Compiles to a Code node (variant `opa`) in the Inflowenger ecosystem.

dataFields.logic_rule:
scope_data := input # the scoped context — fields selected by `scope` are available as input.<field>
criteria := data # values coming from the Conditions key/value pairs — available as data.<key>

result := true

label: Doc Store
description: Read (run a query) or write documents in a referenced Document memory store. A read runs `query` against the store; a write takes its payload from `input` (the node `scope` or an input JSONPath). Compiles to an Extrinsic on `svc.store.doc.{ACTION}` (inflo-fusion listens on `svc.store.doc.*`).
notes: Leave `storeId` "" (the designer picks the store in the drawer — note it) and set `action` to "read" or "write".

A read (`action: "read"`) runs a basic SQL `query`. You do not know the store's columns, so write a simple skeleton with placeholders for the designer to fill: `select * from <STORE_NAME> where <field> = <value>`.
A write (`action: "write"`) stores the payload selected by `input` (a JSONPath, default the node `scope`); no query.

Prefer shaping the write payload with a Cast before this node rather than writing whatever is in scope: put a `cast` node bound to THIS same store in front of the write, and point the write's `input` at what it produced (`$.mapped`). The Cast assembles a clean object matching the table's columns, so the row that lands is exactly the store's schema — no stray Context fields, nothing missing. See the cast kind.

label: Vector Store
description: Read (run a query) or write into a referenced Vector memory store. A read runs `query` against the store; a write takes its payload from `input` (the node `scope` or an input JSONPath). Compiles to an Extrinsic on `svc.store.vec.{ACTION}` (inflo-fusion listens on `svc.store.vec.*`).
notes: Leave `storeId` "" (the designer picks the store in the drawer — note it) and set `action` to "read" or "write".
A read (`action: "read"`) runs `query` — the text to match by similarity: a literal string, or `{{$.path}}` to embed text from the Context (e.g. `{{$.ticket.body}}`).
A write (`action: "write"`) stores the payload selected by `input` (a JSONPath, default the node `scope`); no query.

label: Cast / Mapping
description: Build a value by mapping each target key (from a referenced Document store schema) to a static value or a JSONPath resolved against the run-time context. Compiles to a Plugin node.
notes: Set `storeId` to the Document store whose row you are assembling — its schema columns are the keys to map (leave `storeId` "" and note it if the designer must pick the store).

Each mapping is `{ "key": "column_name", "mode": "static" | "jsonpath", "value": "…" }`: `static` writes the literal `value`; `jsonpath` resolves `value` as a `{{$.path}}` (or `{{$this.path}}`) template against the Context at run time. The assembled object is written under `key` (default `mapped`).

The point of a Cast is to prepare a clean, table-shaped record just before a Doc Store WRITE: Cast (bound to the store) → Doc Store write with `input: "$.mapped"`. It has no output ports of its own, so unlike an LLM/Rule it MAY run on a many-scope — `scope: "$.orders[*]"` builds one mapped record per element, which pairs with a per-element write.

label: HTTP
description: Make an HTTP request to an external API and write the response back to `key`. The method, URL, headers, query params and request body are set on the node; each may embed {{$.path}} context vars, resolved at run time. Compiles to a Plugin node.
notes: Put the request in `body`: `{ "method": "GET|POST|…", "url": "https://…", "headers": [{ "key": "", "value": "" }], "query": [{ "key": "", "value": "" }], "body": "", "body_type": "json" }`.

`headers` and `query` are key/value rows; `body` is the raw request body (a JSON string when `body_type: "json"`); `body_type` (json | form | text) sets the Content-Type. Any field — url, header value, body — may embed `{{$.path}}` context vars, resolved at run time.

label: AI Decision
description: Evaluate a block of state — and any evidence you inject — against typed questions on a decision model, whichever one the settings profile points at. Two wire protocols serve these models and the node speaks both, selected by the profile's `provider`: `systemone` (TypeSafe's hosted Jev, a local Laya, Ollama's `nimble`) and `decisions` (OpenAI's Decisions API on `gpt-6-luna`, and gateways implementing its shape). Nothing about the flow changes between them — the questions, the options and the port tags are identical — so a flow can be re-pointed by swapping the profile. Each question declares the answers it may return — choice options, score levels, or yes/no — and the model returns a probability over every one of them in a single sub-second call, never free text. Every option of a routed question is an output port (tag `<question id>.<option name>`); the top answer's port fires. Use it for the bounded, non-reasoning decisions (classify, triage, gate) that do not need an LLM turn. `body.state` is the subject template and `evidence` the supporting chunks. Compiles to a Plugin node.
notes: `body.state` is the subject to evaluate — the case, the ticket, the message: a text template with `{{$.path}}` context vars. A template that is exactly one `{{$.obj}}` token sends that JSON value as-is.

The protocol, the endpoint, the key and the model all come from the SETTINGS PROFILE, not from the node, so the flow does not name them: `provider: "systemone"` (the default when empty) posts to `/v1/systemone` and defaults to `jev-latest` on `api.typesafe.ai`; `provider: "decisions"` posts to `/v1/decisions` and defaults to `gpt-6-luna` on `api.openai.com`. A profile that names its own `url` — a local server, a gateway — must also name the `model` that endpoint serves.

`evidence` is the optional reference material the decision rests on — the retrieval side of a RAG decision: `[{ "source": "contract.pdf", "text": "{{$.kb.clause}}" }]`. Both fields of each row are templates. With any row present the node sends `state` as `{ "case": <state>, "evidence": […] }`, so a question can cite a part of either by backticked path (`case.problem`, `evidence[0].text`). The service has no separate evidence parameter — this is how evidence reaches it.

Keep state and evidence to what the questions need: they share one context budget (~64k tokens, state plus the longest question inside ~32k) and accuracy falls as it fills with material the questions do not use. Filter before injecting; do not pass whole documents.

Hard ceilings, enforced before the call: at most 64 `questions` and 64 `evidence` rows per node, 255 choice options, and 10 score levels (26 against a local Ollama decider). Exceeding one fails the node with a plain error naming the array — it is almost always a loop or a bad `{{$.path}}` upstream rather than an intended design, so split the work across nodes instead of raising the count.

Each question is `{ "id": "snake_case_id", "type": "choice" | "score" | "noul", "instructions": "the question the model evaluates the state against", "route": true, "min_confidence": 0, "options": [{ "name": "snake_case", "description": "what this option means" }] }`.

`instructions` may instead be an object: the question in one field and the data it needs in the others, cited by backticked name — `{ "question": "Does this breach `policy`?", "policy": "{{$.kb.policy}}" }`. Equivalently, keep `instructions` as text and add `references`: `[{ "name": "policy", "value": "{{$.kb.policy}}" }]` — the compiler assembles the object form from the two (`name` becomes the backtick handle; `question` is reserved for the text).
Every string in a question is a template: instructions (at any depth), each reference `value` and each option `description` have their `{{$.path}}` vars resolved before the call.

`options` per type — choice: one row per selectable option (1–255); score: the ordered levels lowest first (2–10 rows on hosted Jev and on the Decisions API; up to 26 on a local Ollama decider); noul: rows named `yes` / `no` carrying only descriptions (optional). A noul's descriptions are folded into the question text on the `decisions` protocol, whose `predicate` takes no criteria field.

A routed question (`route: true`, the default) turns every option into an output port whose route tag is `<question id>.<option name>` (e.g. `category.billing`, `repeat.yes`); the top answer's port fires. Several routed questions fire one port each. `route: false` keeps the answer as data only (no ports).

The model cannot answer outside the declared options. On `systemone` it also cannot decline: when the state fits none, it still picks one — so declare an `other` option when the state may not fit, as the visible no-match branch. On `decisions` the model MAY refuse a single question while answering the rest; a refused question has no answer and so no port, and a routed one leaves through `_exception` with code `refused`. Declaring `other` does not prevent a refusal, so a flow that must survive one needs the `_exception` branch drawn.

Every node with a routed question also has an `_exception` port: it fires on an API error, a missing answer, a routed question the model refused (`decisions` only), or when `min_confidence` (0 = off) is set and the top answer's confidence falls below it. The reported `code` says which: `provider_error`, `no_answer`, `unbound_option`, `refused`, `low_confidence`.

Transient provider failures are retried before `_exception` fires — 429 and 529 on `systemone`, 429 and any 5xx on `decisions`, which is what OpenAI's own SDKs retry. The budget is the profile's `max_retries` (default 2, `0` to decide once). A bad key or a validation error is never retried.

The full distribution lands under `key` (`answers.<id>.probabilities`, `.confidence`, `.answer`), so a `rule` node after it can apply a policy; prefer that over `min_confidence` when the threshold should be visible on the canvas.

Not a reasoner: no tools, no memory, no chain of thought. `evidence` lets it weigh material you have already retrieved and filtered — it does not go and read for you. When the decision needs multi-step judgment, or the documents themselves have to be searched, use an `llm` node with bound functions instead.

label: Human in the Loop
description: Hand the flow to a person when it cannot settle something itself. The prompt tells the session what to establish — read from the run’s own context — and the questions come out of the conversation, not the canvas. Either park the run until the person is done (it resumes from here) or record the task and carry on. Compiles to an Extrinsic against the backend `hitl` service (`svc.hitl.add`), which records a Human Task surfaced under Operate → Human Task.
notes: `prompt` is the node: it tells the session what to establish with the person and may embed `{{$.path}}` context variables, which the runtime resolves before the task is recorded. Write it to read the run's history and work out what to ask — there is no static question list, because a flow reaches a human exactly when what to ask is not yet known.
`mode` is "park" (the run stops here and resumes once the session closes) or "continue" (record the task, carry on). `channel` is "direct" (only one supported today), "telegram" or "whatsapp".
